rules.statement: Side-effect work that must finish after a change has been committed (such as terminating sessions or revoking tokens) is passed `CancellationToken.None`, while work that runs before the commit keeps the request's cancellation token.
rules.why: Once the change is saved, a client disconnect must not leave the follow-up incomplete (for example, other sessions and their tokens still active). Before the commit, cancelling should cancel the whole operation.
rules.check: Look for post-commit follow-up calls that pass the request's `CancellationToken`/`HttpContext.RequestAborted`, and for pre-commit steps that pass `CancellationToken.None`.

rules.statement: After an administrator resets a password, terminate every session of the account's principal through the session termination service, which revokes every grant and sends back-channel logout. Do not rely on rotating a security stamp.
rules.why: Nothing reads the security stamp, so without this a compromised account's sessions and refresh tokens keep working until they expire. OWASP ASVS V3.3.3 requires terminating sessions across relying parties after a password reset.
rules.check: Look for password-reset paths that only rotate the security stamp, or that don't call session termination (e.g. `RevokeAllAsync`) with a password-reset reason after the commit.

rules.statement: A self-service password change terminates every other session of the principal and revokes every grant not issued under the current session, but keeps the current session.
rules.why: This follows OWASP ASVS V3.3.3 and NIST SP 800-63B, and avoids signing the user out of the session that proved the change.
rules.check: Look for self-service password-change code that leaves other sessions or grants active, or that also terminates the current session.

rules.statement: Blocking an end user terminates all of the principal's sessions (revoking grants and sending back-channel logout) even if it was already blocked, and the block is refused at every subject validation. Unblocking terminates nothing and restores no grant. Consents are kept in both cases.
rules.why: A blocked principal must not keep using existing sessions or tokens, and every token request for it must be refused.
rules.check: Look for block operations that skip session termination when the state didn't change, subject validation that ignores the blocked flag, or unblock operations that terminate sessions or restore grants.

rules.statement: Store authorization-relevant state (such as a blocked flag) as a typed, persisted property, not in a free-form metadata bag.
rules.why: State in a free-form bag is untyped and nothing enforces it.
rules.check: Look for authorization or enforcement flags written to or read from generic metadata dictionaries or property bags.

rules.statement: A migration that adds a new boolean or state column adds it as non-null with a safe default and only expands the schema.
rules.why: Existing rows get a well-defined value, and the migration stays additive and non-breaking.
rules.check: Look for new columns added as nullable without reason or without a default, or migrations that combine the addition with destructive schema changes.

rules.statement: A validation handler that is chained after other handlers for the same command returns at once when the operation already has an error, and is registered with `TryAddEnumerable`.
rules.why: Additional handlers then run alongside the default one without being registered twice, and they don't overwrite an error that is already set.
rules.check: Look for chained handlers that set an error without first checking for an existing one, or that are registered with `AddSingleton`/`AddTransient` instead of `TryAddEnumerable`.

rules.statement: Every management API change to a security-relevant resource is recorded as an audit event.
rules.why: Administrative changes such as blocking or unblocking must be auditable.
rules.check: Look for new management endpoints that change state but don't call the audit recorder.
